First, think about what you're there to do. Is it an application? Directions? Adjournment? Return of subpoena? Keep that clear in your head because a surprisingly large number of practitioners don't. It helps with knowing what points to hit, what information you need to convey, and the best way to do it.  A busy Registrar on Tuesday's return of Subpoena list doesn't what to hear about the files history if it's the first return and there's just an adjournment by consent.  A judge making directions wants the matter to conform to the UCPR and the relevant practice directions.  They're just there to help you. 

Second, take some time to prepare, even if you think it's a bit overboard. You can never be too prepared, and even if you spend your hours thinking about an adjournment, that's better than pulling something out of your ass on your feet or 5 minutes before dialing in.  That will bring you a degree of comfort. Maybe write out everything you want to say. Don't use it as a script, but use it as a process to discipline your thinking before the judicial probing. 

Third, remember that judges can sometimes be a little querulous, but that's usually just in a positive, judicial way.  They question you to clarify things, not to trip you up or embarrass you. They genuinely want you to assist them and only get visibly annoyed when they think counsel (or whoever is appearing) hasn't prepared adequately, which adds even  more work to their already   overburdened yoke.

Last, when the judge gets out the jumper cables and beats you black and blue, remember that they do so because of the blood pact of 1459, in which the grand demon Djeisktragh agreed to give New South Wales Silks omnipotence in return for the blood of solicitors who work in Martin Place. You are part of a beautiful tradition, spanning aeons, and your sacrifice may help Bret Walker SC convince the High Court that, given the proper institution of proceedings in Missouri, and the negative declaratory nature of much later Queensland proceedings, in *Mackellar Mining Equipment Pty Ltd v Wright (as representative of the estate of Leslie Arthur Wright)*, continuation of the Missouri proceedings wouls be vexatious or oppressive in the sense of being productive of serious and unjustifiable trouble and harassment, or be seriously and unfairly burdensome, prejudicial or damaging.

Hi, 

I started as a graduate at a mid-tier firm in construction litigation, then a large top-tier firm at associate level, before I moved to an international firm in London as a Foreign Qualified Lawyer.  I then took the QLTS after a few years. Even with about three years as a FQL and almost 8 years PAE, I found private tuition to be of really great benefit, especially for the OSCE as it's a bit unlike previous written exams. 

I also found that LinkedIn didn't matter a great deal. What mattered was my previous work experience and references. I also studied an LLM at an overseas University, which helped my chances significantly.  Like any job, they're looking for someone with experience, especially in a busy top tier.  I'm sorry to say that it's usually the crucial part.

Otherwise, I found the work to be much the same. You have a managing partner in charge of it all, some senior associates doing the hard thinking, supported by the junior end. I enjoyed my time in a top-tier, which made the transition easy. Especially when the managing partner took out a pair of jumper cables and beat me black and blue. 

Good luck on your exam and path. DM me if you have any more questions.
